Personal Website

Open the R console and set your working directory to your selected directory.

setwd("C:/Users/mirra/OneDrive/Documents/Website_personal")

0.1 Create website skeleton

We will create a website skeleton using a baked-in command from the rmarkdown package.

  • Note the use of ::: in the command below.
rmarkdown:::site_skeleton(getwd())

This will create three files:

  • _site.yml: this is a file we will edit to control meta-features of the website
  • about.Rmd and index.Rmd: these are just template files for pages on the website

The basic design of an R Markdown website is to have a _site.yml file that controls much of the appearance of the website (e.g., the navigation bar, the website theme, directories where files are found/saved, etc…).

Otherwise, each page within the website is created using an .Rmd file.

0.2 Create R Project

Let’s go ahead and make this directory an R Project, because R Studio tends to play more nicely with R Projects.

To do this, go to File: New Project: From Existing Directory and then select the directory where your website lives.

R Studio should be smart enough to figure out that this directory is a website. You can confirm this by looking at the contents of the website.Rproj file. For example, you could open your Terminal, set working directory to your website directory and execute the following command. You will need to replace website.Rproj with the name of your .Rproj file name.

cat Website_personal.Rproj

0.3 Change output directory

This step is not strictly necessary, but is helpful for keeping things tidy.

Open the _site.yml file and add the following line at the end.

output_dir: docs

Recall that GitHub pages likes looking in a folder called docs to find .html files that it serves on a GitHub pages website.

0.4 Render the site locally

We will use a command in the R console to build your website. Open the R Console and execute the following command.

rmarkdown::render_site()

Check the docs folder of your project directory. You should see:

  • about.html and index.html: these are the rendered html documents that make up your website
  • site_libs directory: this contains all the extra bells and whistles that are needed to make your website look pretty on GitHub pages.

All of these files will need to be committed and pushed to GitHub to get your website working.

0.5 Turn off jekyll

In prepartion for pushing to GitHub, we will add an empty file named .nojekyll to your project. This can be done via the Terminal.

touch .nojekyll

This is not strictly necessary, but it may slightly speed up website deployment when you push new material to GitHub. The presence of this file tells GitHub pages that it doesn’t need to rebuild any part of the website before serving the site.

Read more about jekyll here.

0.6 Initialize git

Open a terminal, make sure your working directory is set to your project’s root directory and execute the following command.

git init

This initializes a git repository. Let’s go ahead and create a .gitignore file. As in DATA 550, I like to do this using touch.

touch .gitignore

Open the .gitignore file and add the .Rproj.user directory to the .gitignore. I will also go ahead and add the .DS_Store file that Macs love to create to my .gitignore as well. Prior to saving, my .gitignore will look like this.

.Rproj.user/*
.DS_Store

Now, we can go ahead and make our first commit.

git add --all
git commit -m "first commit"

0.7 Initialize GitHub repository

Now hop over to Github and create a new repository. Do not initialize with a README and a .gitignore.

Add your GitHub repository as a remote and push using the ssh protocol.

git remote add origin git@github.com:benkeser/example_website
git push origin main

0.8 Create GitHub pages website

In your web browser, navigate to your GitHub repository.

Click on Settings. Then on the left hand side of the screen, look under Code and automation and click on Pages.

Leave Source set to Deploy from a branch.

Under Branch, select main, select the docs folder, and click Save.

Your website is now live at https://yourusername.github.io/yourreponame. You can visit that website to confirm.

You can add this website address to your repo description so that it’s easy to find.

1 Personalizing your website

1.1 General workflow

We will now make some updates to personalize your website. The general workflow for updating your site is as follows:

  • Update source code (i.e., .Rmd or _site.yml files)
  • Compile the website using rmarkdown::render_site() to generate new .html files
  • Open docs/index.html to preview website
  • When satisfied with appearance, git commit and git push to update the website online

What you see locally will be what you see on GitHub. If the website renders differently online vs. locally, then there is likely an issue of not pushing updated site_libs to GitHub.

In general, you will not want to update the compiled source code (i.e., the .html files in the docs folder) directly.

1.2 Updating the home page

Let’s add a picture of yourself to the home page. First, make an images directory.

mkdir images

Move a picture of yourself to this directory. My picture will be called profile.png.

Add a code chunk to index.Rmd

```{r, echo=FALSE, fig.align='center', out.width='40%'}
knitr::include_graphics("images/profile.png")
```

Note that we used out.width='40%' to specify relative width of the image. This allows the image to scale with different sized browsers

Getting an image to look nice on a website across all possible devices typically requires:

  • Reasonably high resolution image
  • Moving away from using just markdown to style your page and instead writing html and/or css directly

Note: when you re-build the website, R Markdown will create a copy of your images directory in the docs folder. In general, R Markdown will put any referenced files into the docs directory.

  • This creates some redundancy, but that is ok unless you are uploading very large files.
  • It enables a simple workflow wherein you only edit files in your projects root directory and never directly modify files in docs.

1.3 Adding columns to the homepage

Let’s change the layout of the homepage to have two columns. This is something we will (for now) achieve directly with (mostly) markdown syntax.

Add the following to index.Rmd.

::: columns
::: {.column width="50%" style="text-align: center;"}

```{r, echo=FALSE, fig.align='center', out.width='100%'}
knitr::include_graphics("images/profile.png")
```

## Your Name

:::

::: {.column width="50%" style="text-align: left;"}

Add some text here describing yourself. Add a [link](https://google.com) so we can see behavior later. 

:::

A few notes: * The above is mostly using Markdown syntax; however, some css has crept into the code – this is the style="text-align: left;" bit above. * Notice we have changed out.width='100%' in order for the image to span the entire left column.

You can play around a bit with the formatting, but note that the columns do not have the best “reactive” behavior. If you view them on a narrow device, the text will get smaller so that everything fits on the screen. Nicer behavior might be to have the columns stack on top of one another. This would require integrating raw html and/or css, which we discuss later.

1.4 Updating the About page

We will make some light edits to the About page to include some basic information about yourself.

Remove the auto-generated content and add a few sentences about yourself (e.g., your education background, current jobs, interests, etc…)

1.5 Updating the navigation bar

Let’s now update the navigation bar to include some links to “socials”. We will do this by updating the _site.yml file. I will add a link to my Github. Other links you might want to include:

  • Email (beware spam if listing on a website)
  • Google scholar profile
  • Bluesky/X (if that’s your thing)
  • ORCID
  • Linked In

Open the _site.yml file and modify the navbar section it so it looks like this:

navbar:
  left:
  - text: Home
    href: index.html
    icon: fa-home
  - text: About
    href: about.html
    icon: fa-book-open
  right:
  - href: https://github.com/benkeser
    icon: fa-github

Here, we have added free icons using fontawesome. Check out the R package documentation to see what icons are available.

1.6 Creating a Projects page

Let’s now add a new page linking to some of our projects.

Create a new .Rmd file in your project root directory called projects.Rmd.

touch projects.Rmd

Open this file and edit it to look something like this.

---
title: "Projects"
---

### [DATA 550 website](https://bit.ly/info550)

A jeykll website I built for previous iterations of this class

### [`vaxstrat` R package](https://github.com/allicodi/vaxstrat)

An R package for computing principal effects quantifying vaccine impact on post-infection endpoints.

Before rendering the site, we should add the Projects page to the navbar. Open _site.yml and update the navabar section.

navbar:
  left:
  - text: Home
    href: index.html
    icon: fa-home
  - text: About
    href: about.html
    icon: fa-book-open
  - text: Projects
    href: projects.html
    icon: fa-computer
  right:
  - href: https://github.com/benkeser
    icon: fa-github

1.7 Including a CV or resume

Let’s also add a pdf resume and link to it. Make a new directory in your project directory to hold a .pdf version of your resume or CV.

mkdir files

Move your resume into this folder.

Now update the navbar section of your _site.yml file.

navbar:
  left:
  - text: Home
    href: index.html
    icon: fa-home
  - text: About
    href: about.html
    icon: fa-book-open
  - text: Projects
    href: projects.html
    icon: fa-computer
  - text: CV
    href: files/cv_full.pdf
    icon: fa-paperclip
  right:
  - href: https://github.com/benkeser
    icon: fa-github

2 Styling your website

Now that the basic workflow for adding and doing light styling of pages is done, let’s see how to make the website look fancier using themes and custom css files.

2.1 Add a site theme

The most straightforward way to update the entire appearance of your website is to select a Bootstrap theme.

To do this update your _site.yml file to include a section specifying the theme.

output:
  html_document:
    theme: yeti

There are several default themes:

  • default, cerulean, journal, flatly, darkly, readable, spacelab, united, cosmo, lumen, paper, sandstone, simplex, and yeti (use null for no theme)

Adding type: inverse below the theme line can sometimes change the appearance of each theme as well.

Note: R Markdown websites using Bootstrap version 3. As of the writing of this document, Bootstrap is available up to version 5 with additional features and themes. Use quarto websites to leverage more recent versions of Bootstrap.

2.2 Add custom css

Cascading Style Sheets (css) controls how html content looks. We use css to change colors, fonts, spacing, layout, and other design aspects.

Selectors and rules are the core structure of css.

  • You target elements of your webpage (e.g., p, .class, #id) and define style rules for each element inside braces (e.g., color, font-size, margin).

“Cascading” means that there styles can come from multiple places (browser defaults, external stylesheets, inline styles) and there is a priority for which are used.

We have already been using css under the hood. E.g., Bootstrap is basically just a style sheet that is set up to control each of the elements of your webpage.

Check out docs/site_libs/bootstrap-3.3.5/css/bootstrap.css to see what it looks like. This document is far more complex than what we will use “by hand”, but it gives you a flavor for what css looks like.

If there is a particular element you would like to change, rather than modifying the bootstrap.css file, we can add a new style sheet to our webpage.

Let’s create a new file called style.css.

touch style.css

Open this file in R Studio and add the following.

/* Default link color */
a {
  color: #2C7BE5;  /* pick your favorite color for links */
  text-decoration: none;
}

/* Hover state */
a:hover {
  color: #1A5BB8;  /* pick your favorite color for links when mouse hovers */
  text-decoration: underline;
}

Here, we are just adding two simple custom styles to our website that define the appearance and behavior of links.

Some notes:

  • a is the html element for links. So we are saying select all links and apply the following rules for styling them.
  • color and text-decoration are two style elements that we are controlling
  • All styles for a given target appear between curly braces and all lines end with a semi-colon.
  • We are specifying the color in hexidecimal format. You can use free color pickers to get the hex code for colors that you like.

In general, LLM’s are reasonably good at generating css if you are able to precisely describe the behavior that you want. Use this to your advantage, but double check that output behaves as expected!

2.3 Add google font

We can also add custom fonts using Google fonts. Visit this website to pick a font that you like. Make sure it is a freely available font!

When you have identified a font that you like:

  • Click on the font
  • Click Get font in the upper right corner
  • Click < > Get embed code
  • Click @import
  • Copy the @import line that is shown. You do not need to copy the <style> and </style> tags

For example, if I was importing the Lato font, I would copy:

@import url('https://fonts.googleapis.com/css2?family=Lato:ital,wght@0,100;0,300;0,400;0,700;0,900;1,100;1,300;1,400;1,700;1,900&family=Raleway:ital,wght@0,100..900;1,100..900&display=swap');

Add this line to the top of style.css.

Note: this technically imports all versions of the font. If you want ever so slightly faster loading, you could uncheck some of the boxes on the left of the page before generating the embed code.

Now add the following chunk to your style.css in order to use this font through the body of your document.

body {
    font-family: 'Lato';
}

Note: if you picked a different font, you would need to reference that font instead of Lato in the above.

Here we are telling web browsers to render the entire body of the html document with this font. If you instead only want to change the font of certain elements, you would include the font-family style tag in an entry for those targets.

You could also add additional style tags to this if you would like. E.g., adding font-size: 19px; will make the font larger.

2.4 Style the project page using html

So far we have been styling using markdown syntax. It is also possible to directly include html. Here, we give one example of that by styling the project page to include cards for each project.

We are going to replace the contents of the Projects page with the following raw html.

<div class="row">

<div class="col-sm-6">
<a href="https://bit.ly/info550" class="project-link">
<div class="panel panel-default">
<div class="panel-heading">
<h3 class="panel-title">DATA 550 website</h3>
</div>
<div class="panel-body">
<p>A Jekyll website I built for previous iterations of this class.</p>
</div>
</div>
</a>
</div>
<div class="col-sm-6">
<a href="https://github.com/allicodi/vaxstrat" class="project-link">
<div class="panel panel-default">
<div class="panel-heading">
<h3 class="panel-title">vaxstrat R package</h3>
</div>
<div class="panel-body">
<p>An R package for computing principal effects quantifying vaccine impact on post-infection endpoints.</p>
</div>
</div>
</a>
</div>
</div>

A few notes:

  • Markdown parsing is a little bit annoying here and seems to require no indentation to recognize that this is raw html. It makes the formatting a little annoying.
  • We are using Bootstrap panels to format our projects.
  • The col-sm-6 allows for dynamic resizing and stacking of elements.

This could be further styled as desired using css.

2.5 Add a favicon

A final finishing touch is to add a favicon – the icon that you see in a browser tab for your website.

You can either use an image that you have generated or use a favicon generator. Save the image as a .png or a .ico and place it in your projects images directory.

Create a new file called header.html in your project root directory.

touch header.html

Add the following contents.

<link rel="icon" type="image/png" href="images/favicon.ico"/>

Update your _site.yml file to look like this:

output:
  html_document:
    theme: yeti
    css: style.css
    includes: 
      in_header: header.html

Re-build the website and you should see the favicon appear!

To finalize the project, commit all the new files and push to GitHub!
